title: React Native in 2026: when we still go native
ex: One codebase for both stores is the default. These are the four cases where we don't.
body:
Most mobile apps we build are React Native. One codebase, both stores, a team that can move between web and mobile. In 2026 the framework is mature enough that "is it good enough?" isn't really a question any more.

But we still go native, in Swift and Kotlin, for a minority of projects. Here are the cases.

## When we go native

- **Hardware is the product.** Bluetooth peripherals, camera pipelines, background sensor logging. The bridges exist, but you end up writing native code anyway, so start there.
- **Platform features on day one.** Widgets, Live Activities, App Clips, watch apps. React Native gets these eventually; native gets them at launch.
- **Heavy animation and gesture work.** Reanimated is excellent. A physics-driven, interruptible interaction is still easier to get right natively.
- **An existing native team.** If your engineers write Swift, we write Swift.

## When we don't

Everything else: forms, lists, maps, payments, chat, dashboards. Northloop is a good example. Ride tracking, Strava import, coach chat and a training plan, all from one codebase, with both stores updated on the same afternoon.

> The question isn't "which is better". It's "what does this app spend its time doing".
